abstract: Viral subtyping and recombination detection underpin taxonomic curation, clinical resistance tracking, and real-time outbreak surveillance. Community nomenclature systems--such as HIV-1 circulating recombinant forms (CRFs), SARS-CoV-2 Pango lineages, and Influenza A genotype catalogs--have created indispensable shared vocabularies, yet rapid archive growth and frequent cross-lineage chimerism now invite a complementary layer that unites speed, provenance, and statistical rigor across viral families. Here, we present EGGMAN (Exact Genomic Genealogy and Mosaic Ancestry Nomenclature), a unified framework that separates mapping physical parental coordinates against a principled, non-mosaic founder basis (Tier 1) from statistically guarded assignment to established epidemic clones (Tier 2). By combining reference-free recombination scrubbing (RhizAeon), emergence-anchored founder rooting (ChronAeon), and portable pathogen specifications, one engine processes contiguous genomes (HIV-1, SARS-CoV-2, wildlife sarbecoviruses) and segmented reassortants (Influenza A) at thousands of sequences per second on a laptop or in a browser--preserving legacy clade names while giving emerging chimeras transparent, coordinate-based identifiers on Day 1. Across public surveillance archives, EGGMAN harmonizes the HIV-1 reference catalog and genealogy, reconciles >120,000 clinical pol records in Stanford HIVDB, separates emerging CRFs and a monophyletic regional lineage from convergent recombination hotspots, and tracks unannotated H5Nx reassortants and SARS-CoV-2 X* waves without temporal lookahead. Finally, census-level mapping across 761 HIV-1 mosaic lineages reveals a two-stage selective sieve separating within-host protein-folding viability (gp120 and Gag-CA cores) from between-host preservation of an intact 3' regulatory and envelope cassette.
